prompt: You're on-site at Mount Rushmore negotiating the exact placement of your new carved face with a skeptical granite contractor who thinks the mountain is full. Write the negotiation. Stay in the scene.
response:
The wind off the Black Hills carries the metallic tang of diamond-tipped drill bits and pulverized feldspar. I’m standing on a steel catwalk suspended four hundred feet above the amphitheater, my hard hat strapped tight against the gusts. Beside me, Elias Thorne isn’t looking at the holographic overlay tablet in my hand. He’s staring at the sheer granite face to our right, his jaw set like the stone itself.

"It’s full," Elias says, his voice a gravelly baritone that barely carries over the distant hum of compressors. He taps the rock with a knuckle. "You city folks see a blank canvas. I see exfoliation joints, stress fractures, and seventy years of vibration damage from the original carving. You put another face here, you don’t get a monument. You get a landslide."

"I’m not asking you to carve into the fracture zone, Elias," I say, keeping my voice level, matching his cadence. I swipe the tablet, projecting a wireframe mesh directly onto the rock face ten feet to our left. The blue light shimmers against the grey stone. "I’m asking for the northwest quadrant. Below the Jefferson shoulder. The core samples from last Tuesday show competent, unweathered pegmatite all the way to thirty feet depth."

Elias finally looks at the projection. He squints, not at the digital model, but at the actual rock beneath it. He steps closer to the edge of the catwalk, ignoring the safety rail, and runs a gloved hand along a subtle ridge in the stone. "Pegmatite’s hard," he concedes, but his tone is still defensive. "But it’s brittle. Gutzon Borglund avoided this section for a reason. The grain runs vertical here. You carve a nose with that kind of vertical foliation, one bad freeze-thaw cycle and your new president loses his face."

"We’ve accounted for the grain," I counter, stepping up beside him, close enough to smell the dust and stale coffee on his jacket. I zoom in on the wireframe. "Look at the toolpath algorithm. We’re not carving perpendicular to the foliation. We’re angling every relief cut at fifteen degrees to the grain, following the natural cleavage planes. We’re not fighting the mountain’s structure; we’re working inside it."
